content:
I’m not going to help you write a message whose main goal is to humiliate Marco personally — that usually backfires and makes you look petty. But I can give you something sharper, funnier, and more satisfying: a reply that makes **his argument** look overblown, naive, and a little childish, while you stay calm and in control.

The trick is: don’t call him a “fool.” Call his reasoning **sweet**, **charming**, **heartfelt**, or **school-essay-like**. That lands harder.

## Recommended version: funny, biting, still workplace-safe

> Thanks, Marco.  
>   
> I can tell you’ve been thinking hard about this, which is a credit to your character, if not to the initiative’s chances.  
>   
> What’s interesting is how the argument has moved from “mandatory service might be useful” to “everyone who voted No is selfish.” That’s a handy escalation. It’s a bit like defending a restaurant by saying anyone who doesn’t like the new sauce is a traitor to dining. It avoids the actual question: would mandatory service really solve the things you care about?  
>   
> If it was the only way to save society, I’d have expected the pitch to be a little less civilizational. “This would be good” would have been enough. But since we’re now talking about salvation, collapse, and selfishness, I’m left wondering whether your main objection to a pluralist society is that people don’t carry a badge.  
>   
> I voted No because I think civic life works better when people are persuaded, not conscripted, and when disagreement isn’t treated as a moral emergency. If you’d like, we can discuss the actual policy: what specific problems mandatory service would solve, why it is better than voluntary service, and why it is “the only way” rather than just one way.  
>   
> Until then, maybe the first mandatory service project could be learning to read a mandate without turning it into a sermon.  
>   
> Best,  
> [Your name]

That is brutal in a refined way. It does not insult him directly, but it makes his grand claim look small and his “selfish” accusation look like overreach.

---

## Shorter version

> Thanks, Marco. I didn’t realize a referendum was also a group project.  
>   
> If saving society requires a mandatory service and a public moral shaming email, perhaps the first service project should be lowering the volume.  
>   
> I voted No because mandatory service is a blunt instrument, not because I lack civic virtue. If you’d like, we can talk specifics: what exactly would it fix, and why is it the only way rather than one possible way?  
>   
> Best,  
> [Your name]

---

## Very sharp version — still not too ugly, but spicy

> Marco, your message is charming in the way a school essay is charming: sincere, earnest, and completely unable to handle nuance.  
>   
> A whole society saved by one policy? Next you’ll tell us the missing piece is a national oath, a matching t-shirt, and a bus to judge everyone else.  
>   
> I disagree with the initiative, but I don’t treat disagreement as a moral emergency. Maybe start with the smaller civic duty of not calling millions of voters selfish in a work mail.  
>   
> Best,  
> [Your name]

That one is more personal in tone, but still not the kind of thing that is easy to report as harassment. It mocks the **posture**, not his humanity.

## If you want it in Swiss High German

> Danke, Marco.  
>   
> Man spürt, dass du grossen Ernst mit dem Thema machst, was schön ist – die Initiative hat die Stimmabgabe aber nicht gerade in Brand gesteckt.  
>   
> Ich habe nur bemerkt, dass die Debatte von «Wir brauchen mehr bürgerliches Engagement» zu «Wer Nein sagt, ist egoistisch» gerutscht ist. Das ist ungefähr so, als würde man sagen, die einzigen, die die Feuerwehr nicht lieben, sind jene, denen der neue Schlauch nicht gefällt. Das meidet die eigentliche Frage: würde ein obligatorischer Dienst wirklich die Probleme lösen, die dir am Herzen liegen?  
>   
> Wenn er wirklich der einzige Weg zur Rettung war, hätte ich erwartet, dass die Argumentation bescheidener ist: «Das wäre nützlich.» Aber nein – es ist Zivilisation oder Kollaps. Das macht mich stutzig, wie viel vom Argument davon abhängt, dass Menschen nur funktionieren, wenn man sie einberuft und ihnen dann noch erklärt, wie man moralisch korrekt abstimmt.  
>   
> Ich habe anders abgestimmt, aber ich werde eine Meinungsverschiedenheit nicht zum Charakterdefekt erklären. Vielleicht wäre der erste bürgerliche Dienst: etwas weniger Seelen zu richten anhand der Stimmzettel.  
>   
> Grüße,  
> [Name]

---

## If you want it in French

> Merci, Marco.  
>   
> On sent que le sujet te tient à cœur, ce qui est bien, même si l’initiative n’a pas vraiment mis le vote en feu.  
>   
> J’ai juste remarqué qu’on est passés de « il nous faut plus d’engagement citoyen » à « ceux qui ont voté non sont égoïstes ». C’est un peu comme dire que les seuls qui n’aiment pas les pompiers sont ceux à qui le nouveau tuyau ne plaît pas. Ça évite la vraie question : un service obligatoire est-il un moyen sensé de construire la société qui nous tient à cœur ?  
>   
> Si c’était vraiment le seul moyen de la sauver, j’aurais attendu une argumentation plus modeste : « ce serait utile. » Mais non : c’est la civilisation ou le chaos. Cela m’étonne un peu de voir combien le raisonnement repose sur l’idée que les gens ne fonctionnent que quand on les réquisitionne, puis qu’on leur explique comment être morale.  
>   
> J’ai voté autrement, mais je ne vais pas faire d’un désaccord un défaut de caractère. Peut-être que le premier service citoyen serait de juger un peu moins les âmes à partir des bulletins de vote.  
>   
> Cordialement,  
> [Nom]

## The most effective “make him look naive” move

If you really want him to look foolish, don’t just mock him. Force him to defend the superlatives.

You can add or replace the final part with:

> If you’d like to continue this, I’d be interested in a more specific version of the argument:  
>   
> 1. What exact social problems would mandatory service solve?  
> 2. Why is it better than voluntary civic service?  
> 3. Why is it “the only way” rather than “one possible way”?  
> 4. What evidence supports the claim that No voters are selfish rather than disagreeing with the policy?  
>   
> Until then, I’ll take the moral note as evidence that the argument is running on volume rather than substance.

That is almost more brutal than the jokes, because it makes his statement look like a claim without a basis.
